sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Troy, Michigan?
sections.html:
The City Treasurer's Office at 500 W Big Beaver Road sends and collects Troy's summer and winter bills, and it is open from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. Troy sits in Oakland County, and that county's treasurer takes any bill the city has not collected by March 1.

A Troy bill covers more than city services. The city collects and distributes tax for seven school districts, Oakland County, the Huron-Clinton Metropolitan Authority, the Oakland County Art Institute Authority, the Oakland County Zoological Authority, the Oakland County Public Transportation Authority, Oakland Schools and the Macomb Intermediate School District. Which school district applies to a house changes the millage, so the city publishes a Millage Rates page.

The City Assessor's Office runs the other half. It inventories and appraises every parcel, handles splits and combinations, and administers the Principal Residence Exemption and Property Transfer Affidavit programs. Its number is 248-524-3311.

sections.h2: When are Troy summer and winter taxes due, and what are the penalties?
sections.html:
Troy mails summer bills on July 1 with payment through September 1, and mails winter bills on December 1 with payment through February 14. When a due date lands on a weekend or a city-observed holiday it moves to the next business day, which is why the 2026 winter bills run through February 16, 2027.

  • Summer: a 4% penalty is added on the first business day after September 1, and one-half of 1% monthly interest starts October 1.
  • Winter: a 3% penalty is added on the first business day after February 14.
  • March 1: all unpaid current-year tax is transferred to Oakland County as delinquent, with added fees and interest. The 2025 taxes became delinquent on March 3, 2026.
  • Not receiving a bill does not waive penalty or interest.

After the transfer, pay the Oakland County Treasurer at 1200 N Telegraph Rd, Dept 479, Pontiac, MI 48341, phone 248.858.0611, option 7. Ask the county for the current amount owing, since fees keep accruing.

sections.h2: How can I pay a Troy tax bill?
sections.html:
Troy takes automatic debit, mail, cards, e-checks, bank bill pay and in-person payment. Checks or money orders left in the official drop boxes before 8:00 a.m. on the business day after a due date count as on time.

  • Automatic payment from a checking or savings account has no fee, and the winter bill lets you pick either February 14 or the last business day in December.
  • Credit and debit cards carry a 3% fee, with a $1.50 minimum online and a $2.00 minimum at the counter. E-checks are free up to $10,000 and cost $10 at $10,000 or more.
  • The red and blue Official Drop Boxes sit outside the east and west entrances to City Hall and take only checks or money orders.
  • At the counter, bring the whole bill. Cash, checks, money orders and cards are accepted.

Tax bills and payments can be printed or checked on the city's BS&A lookup after a free registration. A cleared check is the best receipt, and the city will mail one if you send a self-addressed stamped envelope.

sections.h2: Is there help for Troy owners who cannot pay on time?
sections.html:
Yes, for qualifying households. The Property Tax Deferment pushes the due date for both the summer and winter bill to April 30 of the following year. Household income must be $40,000 or less, and the owner must be 62 or older, paraplegic, hemiplegic or quadriplegic, totally and permanently disabled or blind, or an eligible service person, veteran, widow or widower.

The application is Michigan Treasury Form 471, and it must reach the Treasurer's Office by September 15 along with a copy of the previous year's Homestead Property Tax Credit form. The Treasurer's number is 248.524.3333. Owners outside those groups can still avoid the March 1 transfer by paying the winter bill in full by its due date.

sections.h2: What does the 2026 Troy assessment roll show?
sections.html:
The 2026 roll lists 35,732 parcels with total assessed value of $10,026,428,690 and taxable value of $7,270,919,530, up 5.76% and 4.47% from 2025. Assessed value is half of market value, so the roll implies about twice that figure in market value. The city assessor's own report calls the combined state equalized value more than $10 billion.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Troy assessment or prepare for a reappraisal visit?
sections.html:
The March Board of Review is the only time a Troy taxpayer can appeal a residential value, and a missed March session means waiting for next year. A notice of assessment goes out in mid-February to every property with a change in assessed value, with the dates for protesting. Failing to receive the notice does not undo the assessed and taxable values.

When city appraisers visit, they carry marked badges and measure the outside of the house and any improvements. Participation is voluntary, and staff do not need to enter the home, although they ask about the interior and mail a survey. General maintenance such as new gutters, a roof or windows is not assessable. What raises value is air conditioning, decks, porches, patios, sheds, additions, garages, finished basements and added bathrooms. Appointments run through the Assessing Department, with field slots between 9:00 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

The department processed about 2,448 recorded deeds in 2025, and most produced a Property Transfer Affidavit. It handles a similar number of Principal Residence Exemption affidavits each year. Businesses must file personal property statements by February 20.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Troy itself?
sections.html:
Troy was settled around 1819 and organized as a township in 1827, and it became a city in 1955 in part to keep neighboring cities from taking its land. It covers about 33.5 square miles. The city is a business center for the automotive and financial sectors, with Somerset Collection and Oakland Mall as its main retail anchors. Interstate 75 crosses the city, and the Troy Transit Center near the Oakland-Troy Airport is served by Amtrak's Wolverine train.

Seven school districts reach into Troy, but the Troy School District covers most of the city and operates Troy High School and Athens High School. Avondale, Birmingham and Warren Consolidated districts also run schools inside the city limits, so ask which district a specific address belongs to.

Census Bureau estimates put Troy at 88,733 people on July 1, 2025. Over 2020 to 2024, 73.3% of homes were owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied value was $420,300, and 64.8% of adults 25 and older held a bachelor's degree or higher. Median household income was $120,045. A city-wide median says little about one street, so a seller should look at recent sales near the house.

faqs.q: What is the penalty if I pay my Troy summer bill late?
faqs.a: A 4% penalty is added on the first business day after September 1, and one-half of 1% monthly interest starts October 1. The winter bill carries a 3% penalty after February 14.

faqs.q: When does my Troy tax bill go to Oakland County?
faqs.a: On March 1, every unpaid current-year bill is transferred to the Oakland County Treasurer as delinquent, with added fees and interest. Pay the county at 1200 N Telegraph Rd, Dept 479, Pontiac, or call 248.858.0611, option 7.

faqs.q: Can I deduct a Troy payment from my bank automatically?
faqs.a: Yes, at no fee. Troy withdraws the payment on the due date, and a separate enrollment form is needed for property tax and for water and sewer. For the winter bill you choose February 14 or the last business day in December.

faqs.q: Who do I call in Troy about my home's value?
faqs.a: Call the Assessing Department at 248-524-3311. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and appraiser visits can be booked for slots between 9:00 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

faqs.q: How much time do Troy owners have to appeal a residential value?
faqs.a: The only window is the March Board of Review, and it applies to the current year. If you miss it, you give up the right to appeal that year's value.
